extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in magazine/media history
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic profile of New York (magazine), its history, notable editorial practices, digital properties, puzzles/competitions, and business/model decisions. Focused on the magazine as an institution rather than instructions for producing a particular piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary competitions — submission theme and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning in early 1969, for two weeks out of every three, Mary Ann Madden edited an extremely popular witty literary competition calling for readers to send in humorous poetry or other bits of wordplay on a given theme that changed with each installment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hundreds, sometimes thousands, of entries were received each week; winners included David Mamet, Herb Sargent, and Dan Greenburg. Typical entries matched the announced theme and delivered humor/wordplay (example given: an epitaph for Geronimo: 'Requiescat in Apache.'). Madden ran 973 installments of the competition, retiring in 2000. Three volumes of competition winners were published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puzzles and crossword practice (types, frequency, editorial stewardship)
rubrics_metrics.description: New York magazine has long run literary competitions and distinctive crossword puzzles; Stephen Sondheim contributed an extremely complex cryptic crossword to every third issue in the first year, later replaced by Richard Maltby, Jr. For many years the magazine syndicated The Times of London's cryptic crossword and, beginning in 1980, ran an American-style crossword constructed by Maura B. Jacobson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puzzle editorial practice included regular complex cryptic crosswords and an American-style crossword with named constructors/editors (Maura B. Jacobson produced ~1,400 puzzles through April 2011; succeeded by Cathy Allis Millhauser and then Matt Gaffney). In 2020 Vulture began publishing daily 10x10 crosswords by specific constructors; puzzle types and frequency (e.g., every third issue for Sondheim's cryptics) are part of the magazine's established approach to puzzles.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Strategist — editorial policy on branded content and monetization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Strategist does not publish branded content that is paid for by the subject of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Strategist is an expansion of a column aimed at helping readers navigate shopping; it functions as a product-review/affiliate site that generates affiliate commissions when readers purchase recommended products (including participation in the Amazon Associates Program). It runs recurring franchises (e.g., 'What I Can't Live Without', 'Strategist-Approved' gift guides) and experiments (e.g., a holiday pop-up shop), but maintains the stated policy of not publishing branded content paid for by the subject while earning revenue through affiliate advertising.
